description: MarshalX is a multidisciplinary student team passionate about space exploration and innovative technology. We aim to transform complex lunar mission data into an intuitive interactive platform for exploring landing sites, dates, lighting conditions, and communication opportunities through clear visualizations and data-driven insights.
summary: Lunaris is an interactive mission-planning dashboard that lets mission planners, educators and the public evaluate lunar landing sites and dates in seconds. It shows the Sun and Earth positions at any site on the Moon, on any date, in a 3D Moon view and a timeline. It then turns them into simple Go / Caution checks for landing light, power, communications and thermal conditions. Instead of working through several expert tools, a user picks a site and a date and immediately sees whether the combination is viable. If the schedule slips, they can shift by a day or a lunar day and compare again.
details:
Missions to the Moon’s south pole face extreme lighting and communication constraints. A small change in landing location or date can change how much sunlight a lander receives and whether Earth is visible for direct communication. Tools such as Quickmap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons give accurate data, but they are built for specialists and are slow to use when comparing many site and date combinations.

Lunaris closes that gap. The user chooses a landing site from a curated list (for example Apollo 11) or enters custom latitude and longitude, then sets a date and time in UTC. The dashboard shows:

A 3D Moon view with the selected site, the Sun and Earth directions, and spacecraft positions.

A mission panel with a Go / Caution verdict for landing light, power window, comms uplink and thermal conditions, plus Sun elevation, Earth elevation, Sun azimuth and relative solar power on a flat panel.

Time remaining before sunset and Earthset, which is critical for operations.

A timeline of Sun and Earth elevation across the analysis window, with the periods that satisfy both power and uplink thresholds highlighted in green.

Adjustable limits: minimum Sun elevation, minimum Earth elevation, mission length, and a terrain horizon mask.

Quick buttons to move one day or one lunar day forward or back, so planners can immediately see how a schedule change affects feasibility.

Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation come from JPL Horizons ephemeris data. For terrain, we use the LRO LOLA south pole digital elevation model (LDEM_80S_40M). We built a horizon-profile script that computes the terrain horizon at a site and compares it with the Sun and Earth angles to find when each is truly visible. This matters at the south pole, where the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon and crater rims and ridges decide when light and Earth visibility are lost.

Lunaris is designed to work for different audiences. Mission planners get fast scenario comparison. Educators and the public get a visual explanation of why the Moon’s poles are so hard to plan for.
